introduction-people-are-the-most-expensi.core: Salaries are usually an engineering organisation's biggest cost, so headcount decisions are investment decisions. Understanding budget cycles, business cases and allocation strategy is how you get and use people effectively.

first_principles.problem: Managers ask for headcount emotionally ('we're overwhelmed') and are denied, or are given people they deploy poorly.
truths: Fully loaded engineer cost is much higher than salary.

analogy.title: A restaurant's staff costs
analogy.story: The ovens are bought once, but chefs are paid every month; staffing is the main ongoing cost to manage.
analogy.breaks: Headcount isn't the only lever: automation, prioritisation and vendors also expand capacity.

check.q: What is 'fully loaded cost' for an engineer?
check.a: Salary plus benefits, taxes, equity, equipment and overhead, often 1.3–1.7× salary.

the-planning-cycle-the-annual-budget-gam.core: Headcount is mostly allocated in annual (or semi-annual) planning: strategy → top-down targets → bottom-up requests → negotiation → final budget. Miss the window and you wait a year.

first_principles.problem: A manager asks for two engineers in March and learns that this year's budget was locked in November.
derivation: Keep a **ranked backlog** of roles for mid-year opportunities.

analogy.title: Applying to university
analogy.story: There are deadlines; missing the application window means waiting another year.
analogy.breaks: Some companies plan continuously, so learn your organisation's rhythm.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Requests land in the right window.

check.q: Why prepare headcount requests months before the planning deadline?
check.a: Budgets are negotiated and locked in advance, and late requests usually wait until the next cycle.

building-the-business-case-roi-vs-burnou.core: 'The team is burned out' rarely wins headcount. Frame requests as return on investment: revenue enabled, cost avoided, risk reduced or delivery accelerated, with data, alternatives and the cost of not acting.

first_principles.problem: Requests based on overwork are seen as poor management, not as investment opportunities.
truths: Finance compares the returns of competing investments.
The cost of inaction is often hidden.
derivation: **Quantify** the value: revenue, savings, risk reduction.

analogy.title: Pitching an investment to an investor
analogy.story: 'Give me $250k and you'll get $1M back' beats 'I'm tired'.
analogy.breaks: Not everything is quantifiable, so qualitative risk arguments still matter for things like security.

example.title: Reframing a request
flow: ✓ 'Incidents cost $1.2M/yr; one SRE automating top 5 causes saves ~$500k + reduces churn risk'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The request is approved as an investment.

check.q: Why is 'the team is burned out' a weak headcount justification on its own?
check.a: It doesn't show business return, and may suggest a prioritisation or management problem rather than an investment opportunity.

resource-allocation-strategy-run-grow-tr.core: Split engineering capacity across Run (keeping the lights on: maintenance, incidents, compliance), Grow (improving current products) and Transform (new bets). Making the split explicit prevents Run from silently consuming everything.

first_principles.problem: 90% of capacity goes to unplanned maintenance, leaving nothing for growth or innovation, and nobody notices until competitors pull ahead.
truths: Maintenance demands grow with system size.
derivation: **Measure** the current split (ticket labels, time tracking).
**Reduce Run** through automation and debt paydown.

analogy.title: A household budget
analogy.story: Bills (run), home improvements (grow) and savings for a new venture (transform). If bills eat everything, nothing changes.
analogy.breaks: The right split varies by company maturity and strategy.

example.title: Rebalancing an org
flow: Automate toil, pay down top debt

check.q: What tends to happen to capacity when Run/Grow/Transform isn't tracked?
check.a: Run work (maintenance and incidents) silently expands and crowds out growth and innovation.

the-mythical-man-month-trap.core: Brooks's law: adding people to a late project makes it later. New people need onboarding (taking time from existing members), and communication paths grow as n(n−1)/2. Headcount helps future capacity, not an immediate crisis.

first_principles.problem: A late project gets four new engineers, and delivery slips further.
derivation: Use headcount for **future** capacity, not rescue.
For late projects: **cut scope** or **extend time**.
Keep teams **small** to limit communication paths.

analogy.title: Nine women can't make a baby in one month
analogy.story: Some processes have sequential steps that more people can't compress.
analogy.breaks: Well-separated, parallel work with good docs can absorb new people faster.

branches.label: Law
children: Adding people to late project → later

example.title: Communication paths
example.outcome: headcount used where it actually helps.

check.q: Why does adding engineers to a late project often delay it further?
check.a: Onboarding takes existing engineers' time and communication overhead grows, while the critical path doesn't shrink.

headcount-archetypes-choosing-the-right-.core: Not all headcount is equal. A senior or staff engineer, an SRE, a platform engineer, an engineering manager or a specialist each solves different problems. Diagnose the bottleneck first, then request the archetype that addresses it.

first_principles.problem: A team asks for 'two more engineers' when its real bottleneck is a lack of senior technical direction or of management capacity.
truths: Wrong hires don't fix the constraint.

analogy.title: Hiring for a restaurant
analogy.story: If service is slow because of the kitchen layout, another waiter won't help; you need a kitchen designer.
analogy.breaks: Juniors are valuable investments too, but they need senior capacity to support them.

example.title: Diagnosing before requesting
example.outcome: the right people for the real problem.

check.q: Why diagnose the bottleneck before requesting headcount?
check.a: Different roles address different constraints, and the wrong archetype won't improve throughput.
